title: Free printable emergency info sheet for seniors in NJ
dek: One page on the fridge that tells paramedics your mom or dad's medicines, allergies, doctors and who to call. What to write, what to leave off, where to keep it, and a free sheet to print.
keyFacts: NJ Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
New Jersey's POLST guidance says to keep the form near the bed or on the refrigerator. Photocopies and faxed copies are valid.
In New Jersey a POLST is signed by a physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant.
Medicare says to protect your Medicare Number like a credit card. Put plan names, not numbers, on the fridge.
Register Ready, NJ's disaster registry for people with access and functional needs, takes sign-ups online or by calling 211.
body:
An emergency information sheet is one page with the facts a paramedic or ER nurse needs in the first few minutes: who your mom or dad is, what medicines they take, what they are allergic to, which doctor knows them and who to call. Fill it in, keep it on the refrigerator door, and update it whenever a medicine or a phone number changes. Our free sheet below prints on one letter page.

The sheet matters most when your parent can't speak for themselves. That could be after a fall, a stroke, a bad reaction to a new pill, or simply on a night when they are too shaken to remember the name of a heart medicine. A sheet does the remembering for them. It also helps the neighbor, home aide or grandchild who is first on the scene and has no idea who the cardiologist is.

Why keep emergency information on the refrigerator?

Responders know to look there. Many first responder programs tell households to keep medical details on the outside of the fridge door, where they can be found in seconds.

New Jersey examples include the File of Life, a red magnetic pouch with a card listing doctors, medicines, conditions and emergency contacts. The Middlesex County Office of Aging and Disabled Services gives them out. Call 732-745-3295 to ask for one. The Franklin Township Police Department in Somerset County runs a File of Life program too, with the pouch on the fridge door and a sticker on the front door or a nearby window so responders know it is there.

Programs like these come and go by town. Call your county office on aging or your local police department and ask whether they hand out a fridge pouch. If they don't, a clear plastic sleeve and a strong magnet work fine. You can find your county office on our county pages.

The New Jersey Department of Health gives the same advice for POLST forms. Its POLST guidance says to keep the form where emergency responders can find it quickly, usually on a table near the bed or on the refrigerator.

What should go on an emergency information sheet?

Stick to what helps in an emergency. Think of the questions a paramedic asks at the kitchen table, and answer them ahead of time.

  • Who they are. Full name, date of birth, address and anything that affects how to talk with them, like hearing aids, low vision, memory loss or a first language other than English.
  • Health conditions. Heart disease, diabetes, COPD, dementia, past stroke, seizures, kidney disease. Short words are fine.
  • Medicines. Names and doses, including blood thinners and insulin. If the list is long, write "see attached list" and staple a printed list from the pharmacy behind the sheet.
  • Allergies. Drug, food and latex allergies, and what happens (rash, swelling, trouble breathing). Write "none known" if there are none, so nobody wonders whether the line was skipped.
  • Devices. Pacemaker, defibrillator, home oxygen, insulin pump, hearing aids, dentures.
  • Doctors and pharmacy. The main doctor, one key specialist, the pharmacy, and the hospital your parent prefers.
  • People to call. Two contacts with phone numbers that are answered at night, plus the person named as health care representative.
  • Where the paperwork lives. Where the advance directive, POLST and insurance cards are kept.
Write "none known" next to allergies. A blank line makes a nurse wonder.

Should I put my parent's Medicare number on the sheet?

No. Write the plan name only, such as "Original Medicare plus a Medigap plan" or the name of the Medicare Advantage plan, and note where the cards are kept.

A fridge door is seen by visitors, workers and delivery people. Medicare's own advice on your Medicare card is to protect your Medicare Number like a credit card and to give it only to health care providers, insurers and other trusted people who work with Medicare. Leave Social Security numbers, bank details and PINs off the page entirely.

Instead, keep photocopies of the front and back of each insurance card in a "grab folder" in a kitchen drawer, along with the medicine list. Whoever rides to the hospital can take the folder. Our important papers checklist covers what else belongs in that folder. If a scammer calls asking for a Medicare number, hang up. Our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors explains the common ones.

Where should advance directives and the POLST form be kept?

Keep the originals where family can reach them fast, give copies to the people who need them, and write the location on the sheet. A POLST belongs near the bed or on the fridge.

New Jersey has two documents families often mix up. An advance directive is your parent's own document. The state's proxy directive form names a health care representative and directs that the document become part of the person's permanent medical records. Give copies to that representative and to the main doctor.

A POLST (Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is a medical order for people who are seriously ill or frail. In New Jersey it is signed by an attending physician, an advanced practice nurse or a physician assistant, according to the Department of Health. The original, usually printed on green paper, stays with the patient and goes with them if they move to a hospital or nursing home. The state's FAQ says photocopies and faxed copies are valid. Our POLST guide explains who should have one.

The older New Jersey Out-of-Hospital DNR form also remains valid, the Department of Health says. If your parent has one, note where it is. For the bigger picture on wills and powers of attorney, see estate planning basics for New Jersey seniors. This is general information, not legal advice. An elder law attorney can help with the documents themselves.

How do privacy rules work if Mom is rushed to the hospital?

The federal privacy rule known as HIPAA covers doctors, hospitals and insurers. It does not cover a sheet your family keeps, and it lets doctors talk with family in an emergency.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services says that if a patient is not around or can't give permission, a provider may share information with family, friends or others involved in their care if the provider believes, in professional judgment, that it is in the patient's best interest.

A few habits make those calls smoother.

  • At the next checkup, ask your parent to tell the doctor's office, in writing if the office has a form, which family members it may speak with.
  • Put the health care representative's name on the sheet, so staff know who has legal standing.
  • Keep the sheet itself to medical facts. Leave out anything your parent would be upset to have a visitor read, and keep sensitive notes in the folder instead.
  • If your parent has dementia, write it plainly. It tells responders to speak slowly and to call you. Our guide to help after a dementia diagnosis has more.

How often should we update it?

Look at it whenever a medicine changes, after any hospital stay, and at least twice a year. Write the date at the bottom each time so a responder can tell how current it is.

  • Update it the day you pick up a new prescription. Pharmacists can print a current medicine list.
  • Redo it after every discharge. Medicines often change in the hospital. Our guide to when a parent leaves the hospital walks through that week.
  • Check it when the clocks change in spring and fall, the same day you test smoke alarms.
  • Make two extra copies. One goes in the grab folder, one with the family member who lives closest.
Also sign up for Register Ready

New Jersey's Register Ready is a confidential registry for residents with disabilities or access and functional needs, so emergency planners can prepare for storms and other disasters. Families and caregivers can help register. Sign up online or call 211. The state notes that registering does not guarantee help in an emergency, so the fridge sheet still matters.

What else helps responders get in fast?

A sheet only helps if responders can get in the door and find it.

  • Make sure the house number is easy to read from the street at night.
  • Give a spare key to a trusted neighbor and write that person's name on the sheet.
  • Keep a phone within reach of the bed and the favorite chair. Our guide to preventing falls at home covers medical alert buttons and other ideas.
  • Program the main emergency contact as "ICE" (in case of emergency) in your parent's cell phone.
  • If your parent lives alone, read is your parent still safe living alone for daily check-in ideas.

faq.q: Where do paramedics look for medical information in a home?
faq.a: Many first responder programs ask households to keep medical information on the outside of the refrigerator door, sometimes with a sticker on the front door so responders know it is there. New Jersey's POLST guidance also suggests keeping the form near the bed or on the refrigerator.

faq.q: How do I make an emergency information sheet for my mom?

Fill in her conditions, medicines, allergies, doctors, preferred hospital, two emergency contacts and where her advance directive is kept. Date it, put it on the fridge door and keep a copy in a grab folder with copies of her insurance cards.

faq.q: Should I write my dad's Medicare number on the fridge sheet?

faq.q: Can the hospital tell me about my parent if they are unconscious?
faq.a: Yes, in many cases. Naming you as health care representative in an advance directive helps too.

title: Questions to ask before hiring home help for a parent in NJ
dek: A printable checklist of 20 questions for any aide, companion, handyman or instructor coming to your mom or dad's home, plus how to judge the answers, red flags, what to get in writing and money rules.
keyFacts: Agencies placing aides or companions with people 60+ in NJ must register with the Division of Consumer Affairs.
Look up a license or registration at newjersey.mylicense.com or call 1-800-242-5846.
NJ requires a written contract for home improvement jobs over $500.
For 2026, $3,000 or more in cash wages to one household employee generally means Social Security and Medicare taxes are due.
Suspect financial abuse? Call county Adult Protective Services or 1-855-835-5277. In an emergency, call 911.
body:
Before you hire anyone to help your mom or dad at home, ask who employs them, what checks they have had, whether they carry insurance, exactly what they will do, how they want to be paid and who covers when they are out. Then confirm the answers yourself. Our printable checklist below has 20 questions that fit on one page.

This page is the interview. Our companion guide, how to vet someone coming into your parent's home in New Jersey, shows how to look up a license, what a background check covers and how to report abuse. Use them together. The questions work for an aide, a companion, a handyman, a personal trainer, a music teacher or anyone else who will spend time alone with your parent.

What questions should I ask before hiring in-home help?

Start with who they are and who stands behind them, then move to the job, the money and the backup plan. The full list is on the printable sheet at the bottom of this page.

Ask every question every time, even when a friend recommends the person. A friend's good experience tells you about one job, not about insurance, backup or how this person handles a fall. In our October 2026 talks with North Jersey families, the questions they wished they had asked sooner were about who stands behind the worker and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

Ask your parent to sit in on the interview if they can. They are the one who will spend the hours with this person. If you live far away, join by video.

How do I judge the answers?

Good answers are specific and easy to check. Weak answers are vague, change when you ask again, or come with a reason you can't verify them.

You askA good signA warning sign
Who employs you?A named agency with a registration number, or a clear "I'm self-employed""It's complicated" or a first name only
What check was done?What was searched, how far back, and the date"I've been checked" with no details
Insurance?Offers a certificate you can call to confirm"I've never needed it"
References?Two or three recent clients who call you backOnly relatives, or no one reachable
Payment?Per visit, by check or traceable app, with receiptsCash only, or a large amount up front

If the answer is an agency, it should have a state registration. New Jersey treats agencies that place aides or companions with people 60 and older as health care service firms, and the Division of Consumer Affairs registers them. Aides with CHHA certification answer to the Board of Nursing. Look up any number you are given at newjersey.mylicense.com or call Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846. Private instructors, trainers and companions hired directly usually have no state license, so references and insurance carry more weight. Our guide to choosing a home care agency covers agency questions in more depth.

What are the red flags when hiring help for a parent?

Watch for anyone who rushes you, won't put things in writing or asks about your parent's finances early. Any one of those is enough to keep looking.

  • Won't give a full legal name, address or registration number.
  • Refuses a background check or a call to the insurer.
  • Asks for cash only, or for a big payment before any work.
  • Wants to start today and skip the trial visit.
  • Talks about money, wills, bank accounts or "helping with the bills" early on.
  • Discourages family visits or suggests your parent doesn't need you checking in.
  • Showed up unasked, saying they were "in the neighborhood."
  • References can't be reached, or all sound like the same person.
A good helper expects to be asked hard questions. Hesitation tells you something.

Our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors covers the door-to-door and phone versions of these tricks.

What should we get in writing?

A short, plain agreement signed by both sides, with a copy kept by a family member. It does not need a lawyer for simple arrangements, but it does need to be on paper.

  • Full names, phone numbers, and the business name and registration number if there is one.
  • The days, hours and what each visit includes.
  • Anything off limits, like the car, the home office, the bedroom or giving medicines.
  • The rate, any travel charge, how payment is made and when.
  • How much notice either side gives to cancel a visit or end the arrangement.
  • Who to call if the person is sick, and who the family contact is.

Handyman and repair jobs follow stricter rules. Consumer Affairs requires home improvement contractors to use written contracts for jobs that cost more than $500. Under the state's contractor law, your parent can cancel a signed home improvement contract for any reason before midnight of the third business day after getting a copy. Our vetting guide lists what the contract must include.

If you hire a helper directly and control what they do and how they do it, the IRS may treat them as your household employee. For 2026, paying one household employee $3,000 or more in cash wages generally means Social Security and Medicare taxes are due, according to the IRS. New Jersey has its own employer rules. Ask a tax preparer before you start. This is general information, not tax or legal advice.

What are the money rules that protect my parent?

Keep payment in the family's hands, pay per visit or per job, and keep a record. Nobody hired to help should ever touch your parent's checkbook, cards or passwords.

Family money rules

Pay per session or per completed job, never months ahead. Pay by check or a traceable app, never cash. A family member, not the helper, writes or approves every payment. No loans, gifts or "advances" to the helper, in either direction. Never share a debit card, PIN, online banking login or power of attorney.

Good helpers like these rules too. A record of every payment protects an honest worker if questions come up later.

Someone in the family should look at your parent's bank statements every month, or ask the bank about adding a trusted contact to the account. If you think money is being taken, call your county Adult Protective Services or the state line at 1-855-835-5277, and call 911 in an emergency. Every county office is listed in our elder abuse reporting guide. Naming a trusted family member in a durable power of attorney, explained in our estate planning guide, also closes a door a stranger might try to open.

What should happen on a trial visit?

Pay for one short visit before you commit to a schedule. Be there in person or by video, and talk with your parent after the helper leaves.

  1. Clear the counters. Before the helper arrives, put away anything you would hate to see go missing, from rings to pain pills.
  2. Walk through the job. Show where things are, go over the written agreement and point out what is off limits.
  3. Share safety basics. Show the fridge sheet from our emergency information guide and who to call.
  4. Watch how they treat your parent. Do they speak to your mom directly, or only to you? Are they patient when she is slow to answer?
  5. Ask your parent alone. "Did you like her? Would you want her back?" Their comfort counts as much as your checklist.
  6. Decide together. If your parent says yes and the answers checked out, set a start date and a check-in call after the first two weeks.

Expect to hear about transportation, too. Home care staff told us most aides don't drive clients. If rides matter, ask early and confirm whose car and whose insurance would be used.

If paying for help is the hard part, our guide to what senior care costs in New Jersey gives a sense of local rates. Live out of state? A geriatric care manager can do the interviews for you and keep an eye on things.

Before you hire: questions to ask

Tick each one as you ask it. Jot notes in the margin.

The person

Name, phone
Agency or company
License no.
References called

Questions

  • Who employs you, an agency or yourself?
  • Is the agency registered with NJ Consumer Affairs?
  • Are you certified or licensed? What is the number?
  • What background check was done, and when?
  • Do you carry liability insurance? May I see it?
  • Are you bonded? What does it cover?
  • Can I call two recent clients near my parent's age?
  • What exactly will you do at each visit?
  • What will you not do?
  • What is the rate, and is travel extra?
  • How do you want to be paid? Is there a receipt?
  • What is your cancellation policy, both ways?
  • Who comes if you are sick or on vacation?
  • Do you drive? Whose car, and whose insurance?
  • Have you worked with memory loss or falls?
  • What would you do if my parent fell or seemed unwell?
  • How will you keep the family posted?
  • Will you sign a short written agreement?
  • Are you OK with family dropping in?
  • Can we start with a trial visit?

Check before day one

  • License checked on newjersey.mylicense.com
  • Agreement signed, copy kept by family
  • Valuables, checkbooks and spare keys put away

faq.q: What questions should I ask a caregiver before hiring them for my mom?
faq.a: Ask who employs them, what background check was done and when, whether they carry insurance, for two recent references, exactly what they will do, how they want to be paid, and who covers when they are sick. Then look up any license or registration number at newjersey.mylicense.com.

faq.q: How do I hire someone to help my dad at home without getting scammed?
faq.a: Interview with your dad present, call references, confirm insurance with the insurer, sign a short written agreement and start with a trial visit. Pay per visit by check or a traceable app, never cash, and never give the helper his checkbook, cards or passwords.

faq.q: Do I need a written contract with a home helper in New Jersey?
faq.a: For home improvement jobs costing more than $500, New Jersey requires one, and your parent can cancel before midnight of the third business day after getting a copy. For aides, companions and instructors, a short signed agreement is still wise. List the schedule, duties, rate, payment method, cancellation notice and what is off limits.

faq.q: Should I pay a private caregiver in cash?
faq.a: It is safer to pay by check or a traceable app and keep receipts. If you hire someone directly, the IRS may treat them as a household employee. For 2026, $3,000 or more in cash wages to one household employee generally triggers Social Security and Medicare taxes. Ask a tax preparer.

faq.q: What are red flags when interviewing a home aide?
faq.a: Refusing a background check, no full name or registration number, cash only, pressure to start today, early talk about money or wills, and discouraging family visits.

faq.q: Where do I report a helper I think is stealing from my parent?
faq.a: Call 911 in an emergency. Otherwise call county Adult Protective Services or the state line at 1-855-835-5277, and file a complaint about a business with NJ Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846.

title: Guardianship in NJ: how it works for an aging parent
dek: When a parent can no longer make safe decisions and never signed a power of attorney, a New Jersey court may need to appoint a guardian. Here is how the process works, what it costs and the alternatives to try first.
keyFacts: Guardianship cases are filed with the Surrogate in the county where your parent lives.
The complaint needs certifications from two physicians, or a physician and a licensed psychologist, who examined your parent within 30 days before filing.
The court appoints a lawyer for your parent, who must interview them and report on less restrictive alternatives.
Most proposed guardians must complete guardianship training and pass a background screening. Spouses are exempt from the screening.
The Office of the Public Guardian for Elderly Adults (609-588-6500) may serve for people 60+ when no one else can.
body:
Guardianship in New Jersey is a court process that gives one person legal authority to make decisions for an adult who can no longer make them safely. A judge in the Chancery Division, Probate Part, decides the case, and the paperwork runs through the Surrogate's office in the county where your parent lives.

It is meant as a last resort. If your mom or dad already signed a durable power of attorney and an advance directive, you may never need it. If they did not, and they can no longer understand those documents, guardianship may be the only legal way to manage their care and money.

General information, not legal advice

For your family's situation, talk with a New Jersey attorney or your county Surrogate's office.

When does a parent need a guardian in New Jersey?

A guardian is needed when an adult cannot govern themselves or manage their affairs, and no less restrictive arrangement will protect them. A diagnosis such as dementia does not decide it on its own. The question is whether your parent still has enough capacity to govern themselves and manage their affairs.

Families usually start asking about guardianship after a crisis. Say your dad has advancing dementia. He has stopped paying bills, a stranger on the phone talked him into wiring money, and his doctor says he cannot live alone anymore. He never signed a power of attorney. The bank will not talk to you, and he refuses to move. That is the kind of situation where a court may step in.

Guardianship is usually not the right tool when:

  • Your parent can still understand and sign a power of attorney or advance directive. Many people with early memory loss can.
  • Valid documents already exist and the agents named in them are doing their jobs.
  • The real problem is a disagreement between siblings. A court process will not fix that, and it can make it worse.

If you are worried about abuse, neglect or someone taking your parent's money, report it right away. Our guide to reporting elder abuse in New Jersey explains who to call. In an emergency, call 911.

What are the alternatives to guardianship?

The best alternative is a set of signed planning documents, made while your parent can still understand them. New Jersey court rules also require the judge to look at less restrictive options before naming a guardian.

  • Durable power of attorney. Lets a trusted agent handle money and property, and keeps working if your parent loses capacity. It must be signed and acknowledged, usually before a notary. Our estate planning guide explains the details.
  • Advance directive. A proxy directive names a health care representative to make medical decisions. An instruction directive (a living will) states your parent's wishes.
  • POLST. For people with serious illness, a POLST turns treatment wishes into medical orders signed with a clinician. See our POLST guide.
  • Benefit helpers. Social Security can name a representative payee, usually a family member, to manage benefits for someone who cannot. Call 1-800-772-1213. The VA has a similar fiduciary program for VA benefits. Neither one needs a court case.
  • Conservatorship. A court can name a conservator to manage money for someone who agrees to it or does not object. The court-appointed lawyer in a guardianship case must say whether this would work instead.
  • Support without a court. Some families set up a team approach, where a parent makes their own choices with help from people they trust. This is often called supported decision making. Ask an attorney how it would work in your parent's case.
A power of attorney signed today can spare your family a court case later.

If your parent is still able, the most useful step you can take this month is to help them sign these papers. Our guide on how to talk with a parent about getting help can make that conversation easier.

How does the guardianship process work in New Jersey?

You file a verified complaint with the Surrogate in your parent's county, backed by two medical certifications. The judge appoints a lawyer for your parent, holds a hearing and decides whether your parent is incapacitated and who should serve.

  1. Call the Surrogate's office. Ask which forms to use. Many county Surrogates post a guardianship checklist online. The forms ask about your parent's health, assets, family and the type of guardianship you are seeking.
  2. Get two certifications. The complaint needs sworn statements from two physicians, or from one physician and one licensed psychologist. Each must have examined your parent no more than 30 days before you file. A judge can relax that window for good cause.
  3. The judge signs an order for hearing. That order appoints a lawyer to represent your parent if they do not have one, and sets a hearing date.
  4. Serve notice. Your parent, close relatives and other interested people must be notified at least 20 days before the hearing. Your parent also gets a notice explaining they can ask for a jury trial.
  5. The court-appointed lawyer investigates. This lawyer must meet with your parent in person, talk to people who know them, look for existing wills, powers of attorney and health care directives, and file a report at least 10 days before the hearing. The report covers your parent's wishes and less restrictive alternatives.
  6. Complete training and screening. A proposed guardian must complete guardianship training. Most proposed guardians also go through the Judiciary's background screening. Court rules exempt a few people, including a spouse or partner and a New Jersey lawyer in good standing, though the judge can still order it.
  7. Hearing and judgment. If the judge finds your parent incapacitated, the judgment names one or more guardians and spells out their powers.
  8. Qualify at the Surrogate. Before acting, the guardian appears at the Surrogate's office to qualify. That can include posting a bond in an amount the judge sets. The Surrogate then issues the papers banks and doctors will ask to see.

If your parent is an adult who receives services from the Division of Developmental Disabilities, the courts have a separate information packet and forms. Ask the Surrogate which one applies.

What is the difference between limited and general guardianship?

A general guardian makes nearly all decisions for the person. A limited guardian has only the specific powers the judge lists, and the person keeps the right to decide everything else.

New Jersey's court rules allow general, limited and temporary guardianships. The doctors' certifications must address the areas where your parent can still make decisions. Say your mom can no longer handle investments or understand medical risks, but she clearly knows who she wants to visit and what church she attends. A limited guardianship can leave those choices with her.

Courts also separate two kinds of authority:

  • Guardian of the person handles personal decisions such as medical care and where your parent lives.
  • Guardian of the estate handles money and property.

One person can do both, or the judge can split the roles. When there is no family member or friend able to serve, the state's Office of the Public Guardian for Elderly Adults may be appointed for residents 60 and older whom the court has found incapacitated. The office does not file cases itself. It accepts court appointments case by case. Its number is 609-588-6500, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

What does guardianship cost, and who pays?

Expect court fees, the cost of two medical exams and lawyers' fees. The judge sets the fees for the lawyers, which are often paid from your parent's own money.

Court filing fees are modest. The Middlesex, Monmouth and Gloucester County Surrogates all list a $200 fee to file for guardianship of an alleged incapacitated person, plus smaller fees for motions, qualifying papers and reports. Those smaller fees differ by county, so check your Surrogate's fee list.

The larger costs are professional. Under the court rules, the judge may set compensation for the lawyer who filed the case, the court-appointed lawyer and any guardian ad litem, paid "out of the estate of the alleged incapacitated person or in such other manner as the court shall direct." There may also be a bond premium if the guardian manages money. We could not find an official statewide figure for a typical total, so ask any attorney for a written estimate before you start.

If money is tight, call Legal Services of New Jersey's free hotline at 1-888-576-5529 (1-888-LSNJ-LAW) to see if your parent qualifies for free help. Your county Area Agency on Aging must also offer legal assistance for low income adults over 60. Reach it through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737.

What does a guardian have to do after appointment?

A guardian works for the court. You have to keep records, file reports on schedule and act in your parent's best interest, taking their wishes into account.

  • Inventory. A guardian of the estate must list your parent's property within 90 days of appointment, unless the judgment waives it.
  • Annual reports. Unless the judgment says otherwise, the guardian of the estate files a yearly financial accounting with the Surrogate, and the guardian of the person files a yearly report on your parent's well-being.
  • Keep money separate. Never mix your parent's money with your own. Keep receipts for everything.
  • Expect review. The Judiciary runs a statewide Guardianship Monitoring Program. Trained volunteers review guardians' reports on the person's physical and financial well-being.
  • Things can change. If your parent regains the ability to decide for themselves, the court has a process to restore their rights.

Guardianship can be a lot of work on top of caregiving. A geriatric care manager can help you plan care, and our guide to caregiver burnout has places to turn when it gets heavy.

Do I need a lawyer to become my parent's guardian?

You are not required to hire one, but the courts say it is a good idea, especially if the case is complicated or anyone objects. Your parent will have their own court-appointed lawyer either way.

A lawyer who handles guardianships often can tell you whether you need one at all, or whether a power of attorney is still possible. Our guide to finding an elder law attorney in New Jersey lists county bar referral lines and questions to ask. If your parent's money is being spent down for nursing home care, the same lawyer can usually help with NJ FamilyCare and MLTSS planning too.

faq.q: How do I get guardianship of my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: You file a verified complaint with the Surrogate in the county where your mom lives, with sworn certifications from two physicians, or a physician and a licensed psychologist, who examined her within 30 days before filing. The court appoints a lawyer for her, holds a hearing and decides whether she is incapacitated and who should serve. Most families work with an attorney.

faq.q: Can I avoid guardianship for my dad with dementia?
faq.a: Often, yes, if he can still understand and sign a durable power of attorney and an advance directive. Many people with early memory loss can. Talk with an elder law attorney soon, because once he loses that ability, guardianship may be the only option.

faq.q: How much does guardianship cost in NJ?
faq.a: Surrogate filing fees are modest. Middlesex, Monmouth and Gloucester counties list $200 to file, plus small fees for motions and reports that differ by county. The bigger costs are the medical exams and lawyers' fees, which the judge sets and which are often paid from the parent's own money. Ask any attorney for a written estimate.

faq.q: What is a limited guardianship?
faq.a: A limited guardian has only the powers the judge lists, such as managing money or making medical decisions. The person keeps the right to make every other decision. New Jersey court rules allow general, limited and temporary guardianships.

faq.q: Who becomes guardian if no family member can serve?
faq.a: For residents 60 and older whom the court has found incapacitated, the state's Office of the Public Guardian for Elderly Adults may accept the appointment. It does not file cases itself. Call 609-588-6500, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.

faq.q: Does a guardian have to report to the court?
faq.a: Yes. Unless the judgment waives it, a guardian of the estate files an inventory within 90 days and a yearly financial accounting, and a guardian of the person files a yearly well-being report with the Surrogate. Volunteers in the Judiciary's Guardianship Monitoring Program review these reports.

body:
Medicare gives almost every nursing home in New Jersey a rating from one to five stars on its Care Compare website. Five stars means quality well above average. One star means quality well below average. There is an overall rating plus three separate ratings for health inspections, staffing and quality measures, and each one tells you something different.

The stars are a good first filter, and they work best alongside other sources. New Jersey's Department of Health posts inspection results and staffing data for every nursing home in the state, and the state's Long-Term Care Ombudsman can answer questions and take complaints at 1-877-582-6995. Below is how to read each source, what to ask on a tour and which warning signs should send you to the next name on your list.

What do Medicare's nursing home star ratings mean?

They compare nursing homes against each other on inspections, staffing and resident care. A home with more stars did better on those measures than most homes in New Jersey or the country.

You find them on Medicare Care Compare. Search by town or ZIP code, then open a home's page to see four ratings.

RatingWhat it is based on
Health inspectionsProblems found in the two most recent yearly state inspections, plus complaint and infection control inspections over the last three years. Serious and widespread problems count more.
StaffingNurse and aide hours per resident each day, registered nurse hours, weekend staffing and how many nurses and administrators left over a year. The data comes from payroll records.
Quality measuresHow residents are doing, such as pressure ulcers, urinary tract infections, loss of the ability to walk and, for short-stay rehab patients, how well they can care for themselves at discharge. Based on resident assessments and Medicare claims.
OverallStarts from the inspection rating, then moves up or down based on staffing and quality.

The health inspection stars are graded on a curve within each state. In New Jersey, the top 10 percent of homes get five stars and the bottom 20 percent get one star. So a three-star home is in the middle of the pack for New Jersey, which is useful to know when you compare a home here with one across the river in New York or Pennsylvania.

CMS, the agency that runs Medicare, says plainly that no rating covers everything. It points out that a home close enough for family to visit often may serve your parent better than a higher-rated one far away.

How is the overall star rating calculated?

The overall rating starts with the health inspection stars, then adds or subtracts at most one star each for staffing and quality measures. Inspections carry the most weight because trained surveyors actually went into the building.

  1. Start with inspections. A home with three inspection stars starts at three.
  2. Adjust for staffing. Five staffing stars add one. One staffing star takes one away.
  3. Adjust for quality. Five quality stars add one. One quality star takes one away.

There are limits. A home with a one-star inspection rating can climb only one star overall, however good its other numbers look. That is why you should always open the separate ratings. A four-star home with two inspection stars and five quality stars is a different place from a four-star home with four inspection stars.

Watch for three symbols on Care Compare.

  • Abuse icon. Marks homes cited for abuse of residents in recent inspections. These homes are capped at two inspection stars, and at four stars overall.
  • Special Focus Facility warning. Homes in this federal program have a history of serious problems and are inspected more often. They get no star ratings at all while in the program. A yellow warning sign shows instead.
  • Trophy icon. New in fall 2026. CMS adds a trophy next to the five stars of high performers, homes with fewer citations, higher staffing and strong results on other quality measures.
Open the three separate ratings. The overall number can hide a weak inspection record.

Where can I read New Jersey inspection reports?

Read them on Care Compare under "Inspections" and on the New Jersey Department of Health's Nursing Home Facility Data dashboard. The state retired its own nursing home report card and now points families to the federal star ratings.

The Department of Health inspects nursing homes for both the state and Medicare. Its Nursing Home Facility Data dashboard lets you search by name or county and see survey results, owner financial statements, infections and staffing levels. You can filter by star rating, Special Focus status, payment type and specialty, such as dementia care or ventilator care.

When you read an inspection report, look past the count of citations.

  • Harm. Citations where residents were actually harmed or put in immediate danger matter most. New Jersey's Division of Aging Services describes level G, H and I violations as actual harm, and J, K and L as immediate jeopardy.
  • Patterns. The same problem cited inspection after inspection, such as falls, bed sores or medication errors, tells you it is not getting fixed.
  • Complaints. Citations from complaint investigations come from families and residents who called the state. Several in a short time are worth asking about.
  • Dates. A bad inspection three years ago followed by two clean ones is a different story from a recent decline.

Ask the administrator about anything that worries you. A good home will explain what happened and what changed.

How do I check staffing at a New Jersey nursing home?

Start with the staffing stars and the hours per resident on Care Compare, then ask the home directly. New Jersey law sets minimum ratios of direct care staff to residents on every shift.

Under state law (N.J.S.A. 30:13-18), every nursing home must have at least:

ShiftMinimum direct care staff
Day1 certified nurse aide for every 8 residents
Evening1 direct care staff member for every 10 residents, at least half of them nurse aides
Night1 direct care staff member for every 14 residents

These are floors. On Care Compare, compare a home's total nurse hours per resident per day with the state average shown beside it. Look closely at weekend hours, which tell you whether the home is thinly staffed on Saturdays and Sundays, and at turnover. High turnover means residents keep meeting new faces, which is hard on anyone, and especially on someone with dementia.

On a visit, ask how many aides work the floor your parent would live on during each shift, how much the home relies on agency staff, and how long the director of nursing and the administrator have been there.

What should we ask on a nursing home tour?

Ask about the care your parent actually needs, who will provide it and how the home handles problems. Then go back at a different time, unannounced, and see if the answers hold up.

Medicare publishes a free printable nursing home checklist. These are good questions to start with.

  • Do you have a bed for long-term care, short-term rehab or both? Will my parent have to change rooms if the stay becomes long term?
  • Do you accept Medicaid, and can my parent stay if their money runs out? Get the answer in writing. Our MLTSS guide explains how Medicaid pays for nursing home care in New Jersey.
  • Do you have a dementia unit? What training do aides have for residents with memory loss?
  • Who is the doctor here, and how often do they see residents? Can my parent keep their own doctor?
  • How do you prevent falls and bed sores? What happens after a fall?
  • How do you use antipsychotic medicines? How often are medicines reviewed?
  • What activities happen on a weekday and on a weekend? Can I see this week's calendar?
  • Is there a family council? How do you tell families about changes in care?
  • Which hospital do you send residents to?

Use your senses on the visit. Notice whether residents are up, dressed and engaged or parked in hallways. Notice how staff talk to residents, how long call lights stay on, how the place smells and what the food looks like. Try to visit at mealtime and again in the evening.

If your parent is being discharged from a hospital to rehab, you may have only a day or two to choose. Our hospital discharge guide explains what to ask before you agree to a facility.

What are the red flags?

The clearest warning signs are a Special Focus or abuse icon, repeated citations for harm, high turnover and staff who dodge your questions.

  • One star for health inspections, or a falling rating over the past year or two.
  • Repeat citations for the same problem, especially falls, pressure ulcers, medication errors or infection control.
  • Staffing hours well below the state average, very low weekend staffing, or a new administrator every year.
  • Residents who look unkempt, call lights that ring for a long time, or strong odors that linger.
  • Pressure to sign quickly, or an admission agreement that asks a family member to personally guarantee payment. Ask what you are signing and have someone review it if you are unsure.
  • Vague answers about Medicaid, staffing or recent inspection findings.

For a broader look at care settings, see nursing home vs. memory care and what senior care costs in New Jersey. If the decision feels overwhelming, a geriatric care manager knows local homes and can help you compare them.

Who can help if something goes wrong after move-in?

Talk to the charge nurse or administrator first. If that does not work, call the New Jersey Long-Term Care Ombudsman or the Department of Health complaint line. In an emergency, call 911.

Who to call in New Jersey

Long-Term Care Ombudsman: 1-877-582-6995, or the online form at nj.gov/ooie. Callers may stay anonymous.
Department of Health complaints about care in a licensed facility: 1-800-792-9770.
Someone at risk of immediate harm: call 911 or local police.

The Ombudsman is an independent state office that advocates for residents. It investigates allegations of abuse, neglect, exploitation and serious injury in nursing homes, assisted living and other long-term care settings, and works to resolve or refer complaints. By law, case files are closed to the public. The Department of Health licenses and inspects the homes and can cite them.

Keep notes as you go. Write down dates, names, what you saw and who you told. If you suspect abuse or financial exploitation, our guide to reporting elder abuse in New Jersey explains each step.

faq.q: How do I check a nursing home's rating for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Go to Medicare Care Compare (medicare.gov/care-compare), choose nursing homes and search by town or ZIP code. Open each home's page to see the overall rating and the separate ratings for health inspections, staffing and quality measures. Then look up the same home on the NJ Department of Health's Nursing Home Facility Data dashboard for survey results and staffing.

faq.q: Is a five-star nursing home always the best choice?
faq.a: No. CMS, which runs Medicare, says no rating covers everything, such as specialty dementia care or how easy it is for family to visit. A nearby home your family can visit often may be a better fit than a higher-rated home far away. Use the stars to build a short list, then visit.

faq.q: Does New Jersey still publish its own nursing home report card?
faq.a: No. The NJ Department of Health says its report card was replaced by the federal Five-Star Rating System on Care Compare. The department does run a Nursing Home Facility Data dashboard with inspection results, staffing levels, infections and owner financial statements.

faq.q: What are the minimum staffing rules for New Jersey nursing homes?
faq.a: State law requires at least one certified nurse aide for every eight residents on the day shift, one direct care staff member for every 10 residents on the evening shift and one for every 14 residents at night. These are minimums. Compare a home's hours per resident on Care Compare with the state average.

faq.q: Who do I call if I'm worried about my dad's care in a nursing home?
faq.a: Start with the charge nurse or administrator. If the problem is not fixed, call the NJ Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 or the Department of Health complaint line at 1-800-792-9770. If he is in immediate danger, call 911.

faq.q: What does the Special Focus Facility warning mean?
faq.a: It marks a nursing home in a federal program for homes with a history of serious quality problems. These homes are inspected more often and do not get star ratings while in the program. A yellow warning sign appears on Care Compare instead.

title: Grief support in NJ after losing a spouse or parent
dek: Free hospice bereavement help, support groups and helplines across New Jersey, how to help a widowed parent, and when grief needs more care.
keyFacts: Medicare-certified hospices must offer bereavement services to the family for up to one year after a patient's death.
The NJ Self-Help Group Clearinghouse helps you find support groups: 1-800-367-6274, open daily 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
NJ Mental Health Cares offers free, confidential emotional support and referrals: 1-866-202-4357, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily.
Medicare Part B covers counseling with licensed therapists, including clinical social workers and mental health counselors.
In a crisis, call or text 988, any time of day.
body:
If your loved one was in hospice, the hospice is required to offer grief support to the family for up to a year after the death. Call the hospice and ask for its bereavement coordinator. If there was no hospice, New Jersey has free statewide lines that can help. The NJ Self-Help Group Clearinghouse at 1-800-367-6274 finds support groups, and NJ Mental Health Cares at 1-866-202-4357 offers free, confidential emotional support and referrals.

Losing a husband, wife or parent can leave you heavy, foggy and worn out. There is no right way to do it and no deadline. This guide covers where to find support in New Jersey, what to watch for in yourself or your mom or dad, and the small things that help. Take what is useful and leave the rest for another day.

Is what I'm feeling normal?

Almost certainly. The National Institute on Aging (NIA) says people in mourning may feel numb, shocked or afraid, guilty for being the one still alive, or even angry at the person who died. All of that is normal.

Grief shows up in the body too. The NIA lists trouble sleeping, little interest in food, problems concentrating and a hard time making decisions. Many people cry easily for a while.

For most people the sharpest pain eases with time. There will still be good days and bad days. Birthdays, anniversaries and holidays can bring a wave of it back. Laughing at a joke or enjoying a visit with a friend can bring a surprising rush of guilt. That is common too, and it does not mean you loved the person any less.

If you are an adult child, you may be grieving one parent while worrying about the other. You may also be handling the paperwork. Our checklist for when a parent dies in New Jersey breaks the practical steps into the first days, weeks and months, so you can set some of it down.

What grief support does hospice offer after a death?

Federal rules require every Medicare-certified hospice to make bereavement services available to the family for up to one year after the patient dies. Grief and loss counseling for the family is part of the Medicare hospice benefit.

Under those rules, the hospice must:

  • Run an organized bereavement program supervised by someone with training or experience in grief counseling
  • Write a bereavement plan of care that says what support it will offer and how often
  • Shape that support around what the family actually needs

What this looks like varies by hospice, so ask what yours offers. If no one has reached out, call and ask for the bereavement coordinator. You are not imposing. This is part of their job.

The NIA also notes that you can ask a hospice for bereavement support even if your family did not use hospice before the death. Ask hospices near you whether they run grief groups open to the public.

To understand how hospice works before a death, see our guide to hospice and palliative care in New Jersey.

Where can I find a free grief support group in New Jersey?

Start with one phone call to the NJ Self-Help Group Clearinghouse. It helps people find and start support groups of all kinds across the state.

  • NJ Self-Help Group Clearinghouse: 1-800-367-6274, open daily 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., or njgroups.org. Ask for grief or widowed persons groups near your town, or groups that meet online.
  • Hospitals, hospices and funeral homes. The NIA suggests checking with local hospitals, senior centers, nursing homes, religious groups, funeral homes and your doctor.
  • Faith communities. Many churches, synagogues and mosques hold grief groups, and clergy can be a comfort. Call the office and ask.
  • GriefShare. These groups are hosted mostly by churches, in person and online. Each week starts with a 30-minute video, then discussion. Groups run in 13-week cycles, and you can join at any point. GriefShare says the cost ranges from free to about $25 for the workbook. The program includes Christian content. Search for a group at griefshare.org.
  • Your county. Each county's office on aging knows local programs. Reach it through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, or find it on our county pages. You can also dial 2-1-1.

Senior centers are worth a look too, even if they do not run a grief group. A standing lunch or class gives the week a shape. Our guide to your first visit to a senior center explains what to expect.

If you were a family caregiver for a long time, the end of caregiving brings its own kind of loss. If you belonged to one of the caregiver support groups in New Jersey, ask whether you can keep coming. The people there already know your story.

You do not have to talk at a first meeting. Listening counts.

How do I help my mom or dad after the other parent dies?

Keep coming around after the funeral, when the casseroles stop and the house gets quiet. Those weeks are often the loneliest.

  • Talk about the person. The NIA says many people find it helps to talk directly about the loss and say the name of the person who died. Share stories. Your parent may be waiting for someone to bring it up.
  • Help with the jobs the other spouse did. Many couples split tasks. One paid the bills and handled the car, the other cooked. Learning the other half takes time. Sit together with the bills, or set up automatic payments for the basics.
  • Watch the meals. Grieving people often lose interest in cooking. Plan regular lunches, drop off food, or look at Meals on Wheels in New Jersey.
  • Help them feel safe at home. Living alone for the first time can feel scary, especially at night. The NIA suggests making sure door and window locks work. Our guide to whether a parent is safe living alone has a fuller checklist.
  • Guard against scams. A recent death can bring calls about debts or offers that sound urgent. Family members usually do not owe a relative's debts from their own money. See our guide to scams targeting New Jersey seniors.
  • Go slowly on big decisions. Selling the house or moving can wait until the first shock passes, unless safety or money forces the issue.

Survivor benefits from Social Security may also matter. The when a parent dies checklist explains the $255 death payment and survivor benefits.

When is grief more than grief?

For most people, grief eases over time without treatment. For some, it stays intense and gets in the way of daily life. If that is happening, a counselor can help, and Medicare helps pay.

The American Psychiatric Association calls this prolonged grief disorder. For adults, it is diagnosed only when the loss was at least a year ago and at least three of its signs have shown up nearly every day for the past month. Signs include feeling that part of yourself has died, intense loneliness, deep emotional pain, trouble getting back to friends and plans, and feeling that life has no meaning. The APA estimates that 4 to 15 percent of bereaved adults have these lasting symptoms. Therapy based on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) has been shown to help.

You do not have to wait a year to talk to someone. Signs it is time to call a doctor or counselor include:

  • Not eating, not sleeping, or not getting dressed for days at a time
  • Drinking more to get through the day
  • Pulling away from everyone
  • Saying things like "there's no point anymore"

What Medicare covers. Medicare Part B covers outpatient counseling with psychiatrists and other doctors, clinical psychologists, clinical social workers, nurse practitioners, marriage and family therapists, and mental health counselors. After the Part B deductible, you generally pay 20 percent of the Medicare-approved amount. One depression screening a year at a primary care office costs nothing if the provider accepts assignment. Visits can happen by telehealth.

Help finding a counselor. NJ Mental Health Cares, a service of the Mental Health Association in New Jersey funded by the state, gives free, confidential emotional support and referrals. Call 1-866-202-4357, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., seven days a week.

If you or your parent is in crisis

Call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day. You can also call if you are worried about someone else. In a medical emergency, call 911.

What helps in the first weeks and months?

Small, steady habits help most. These ideas come from the NIA's advice for people in mourning.

  • Keep up with the doctor. Grief is hard on the body. Book a checkup and tell the doctor what has happened.
  • Eat with people when you can. If meals at home feel too quiet, have lunch with a friend or turn on the radio.
  • Move a little each day. A walk around the block counts. Our exercise at home guide has gentle options.
  • Return to something you enjoy. Painting, music, a card game or a club can lift a mood, even briefly. When you feel ready, volunteering can give the week a purpose.
  • Sort belongings slowly. Try three piles: keep, give away and not sure. Ask family to help, and set aside a few special items for children or grandchildren.
  • Go at your own pace socially. Low-key outings like a walk or a movie are a good start. It is fine to make the first call.

Loneliness after a loss is real and common. Our guide to staying connected in New Jersey lists ways to see people regularly, from phone check-in programs to clubs and classes.

faq.q: How do I find a grief support group for my mom in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the NJ Self-Help Group Clearinghouse at 1-800-367-6274 and ask for grief or widowed persons groups near her town or online. Also ask the hospice that cared for your parent, local hospitals, senior centers, her faith community and the funeral home.

faq.q: How long does hospice grief support last?
faq.a: Federal rules require a Medicare-certified hospice to make bereavement services available to the family for up to one year after the patient's death. Call the hospice and ask for the bereavement coordinator.

faq.q: Can I get grief support from a hospice if my parent was not in hospice?
faq.a: Often, yes. The National Institute on Aging says you can ask hospice workers for bereavement support even if hospice was not used before the death. Ask hospices near you whether their groups are open to the public.

faq.q: Does Medicare pay for grief counseling?
faq.a: Grief counseling for the family is part of the Medicare hospice benefit. Outside hospice, Medicare Part B covers outpatient counseling with psychologists, clinical social workers, marriage and family therapists and mental health counselors. You generally pay 20 percent after the Part B deductible.

faq.q: How do I help my dad after my mom died?
faq.a: Keep visiting after the funeral, talk about your mom and say her name, help with the tasks she used to handle, and watch that he is eating and sleeping. Encourage a checkup with his doctor. If he seems stuck in deep grief or talks about having no reason to go on, call or text 988 for guidance.

faq.q: When should grief be checked by a doctor?
faq.a: Talk to a doctor or counselor if grief keeps someone from eating, sleeping, getting dressed or seeing people, or if they are drinking more to cope. Prolonged grief disorder is diagnosed in adults when intense grief lasts at least a year and gets in the way of daily life. Therapy can help.
